newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Crime-ridden S.Africa plans private sector jails.
newsitem.headline: Crime-ridden S.Africa plans private sector jails.

text.p: South Africa, grappling with a spiralling crime wave and overcrowded prisons, is inviting the private sector to build new jails.

Tender documents asking companies to bid for the financing, design, construction and operation of four new prisons will be issued on May 21, a Correctional Services department spokesman said on Monday.

The government is looking for private firms to build two maximum-security jails each for 1,500 prisoners in Northern Province and the Free State, a similar-sized facility for prisoners awaiting trial in Gauteng and a further unit for 800 youth offenders in the Mpumalanga region.
The closing date for bids is June 25 and construction of the new penal units is due to start in October.
Other private jails could follow, putting South Africa at the forefront of prison privatisation, following the example set by the United States, Britain and Australia.

"The whole idea is based on the assumption that government will not have the money to "build the kind of (prison) faciltiies needed," CorrectionaL Services Minister Sipo Mzimela said earlier this year.
Overseas prison and security groups like Britain's Group Four and U.S. firms Correctional Services Corp and Wackenhut Corp are expected to show interest in the project.

Many of South Africa's existing prisons are severely run-down and overcrowding is a major problem, with the number of prisoners exceeding the design capacity of the country's jails by around 50 percent.
The prison population has risen from 125,000 at the end of 1996 to over 130,000 at present while escapes are running around 100 a month, one of the highest rates in the world.
Since President Nelson Mandela won the country's first all-race elections in 1994, political violence has dropped dramatically but criminal violence has soared.
Police figures show 1.8 million crimes were reported in South Africa last year. South African banks estimate that robberies cost the industry some $25 million a year.
